clue.text: Labour beginning to examine provocateur's white paper

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept from examine

blocks.note: labour as a noun is hard work, toil
its first letter
an online provocateur who posts to stir up anger is a troll

explanation.surface: A government's white paper on employment is opened up to scrutiny by an agitator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'White paper' looks like a government policy document; read literally it is the stuff on the roll in the bathroom.
explanation.definitionFit: Lavatory tissue is a household paper normally sold in white, so the literal phrase describes it.

clue.text: Low-ranking office worker behind incomplete work

blocks.note: a temp is a temporary office worker
behind schedule means late

explanation.surface: A junior clerk is running late with a half-finished task.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Incomplete work' reads as the temp's unfinished job, but it is the definition: a pattern with blanks still to fill.
explanation.definitionFit: A template is a ready-made framework or document that still has to be filled in before use.

clue.text: Working together like many a football team

blocks.note: first meaning: colluding, allied with someone
second meaning: belonging to a competition table, as most clubs do

explanation.surface: Teamwork is compared with the way a football side plays together.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in league with someone is to collude, and literally most football clubs play within a league.

clue.text: Relaxes with cups and saucers, repeatedly taking time out

indicators.note: taking something out more than once removes every occurrence of it

blocks.note: cups and saucers make up tea sets
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Someone unwinds over teacups and keeps taking time off.
explanation.walkthrough: Both Ts go, the first and the one in the middle, which is why the clue says 'repeatedly'.
explanation.definitionFit: To ease is to slacken or loosen, so eases matches relaxes as a third-person verb.

clue.text: Engineers do their own version of Get Back

blocks.note: the Royal Engineers, a British Army corps
to cover a song is to record one's own version of it

explanation.surface: A band of engineers records its own rendition of the Beatles song Get Back.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals make Get Back look like the Beatles' title only; it is just the phrasal verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To get back something lost is to regain or retrieve it.

clue.text: Wise poet - Homer's neighbour

blocks.note: Edward Lear, the nonsense poet
Ned Flanders lives next door to Homer Simpson in The Simpsons

explanation.surface: A sage poet is said to live beside the Greek epic poet Homer.
explanation.walkthrough: Homer looks like the ancient Greek poet, which suits 'poet', but the Homer meant is the cartoon father.
explanation.definitionFit: Learned means having much knowledge from study, scholarly, close to wise.

clue.text: One way to run a mile without problems

blocks.note: taken as written
M is the abbreviation for mile
OK means all right, with nothing wrong

explanation.surface: Someone describes running a mile with no trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'run' about athletics; the definition uses the idiom 'run amok', so the answer is a manner in which one can run.
explanation.definitionFit: To run amok is to behave wildly, so the word is literally one manner of running in that idiom.

clue.text: Thief supposedly cleaned up image to win power

indicators.note: cleaning something up reorganises it, so the letters are rearranged
to win something is to gain and hold it, so the jumbled word takes the next letter inside

blocks.note: taken as written
P is the abbreviation for power

explanation.surface: A crook burnishes his public image to gain power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supposedly' is there because the bird's reputation for stealing shiny things is folklore rather than fact.
explanation.definitionFit: The magpie is reputed to steal glittering objects, and the word also means a petty hoarder or pilferer.

clue.text: One member of team upset exercise group, I'm afraid

indicators.note: in a down clue upsetting something turns it upside down, so the letters read from the bottom up

blocks.note: a rep is one repetition of a gym movement, done in sets
eek is a cry of fright

explanation.surface: A worried member of a team says their exercise class has been disrupted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'm afraid' reads as a polite apology but supplies a squeal of fright. The parsing of 'exercise group' is uncertain; REP is the only reading that fits the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A keeper is a goalkeeper or wicketkeeper, a single position in a football or cricket side.

clue.text: Wiggling ends, pair did twist

indicators.note: wiggling things are moved about, so these letters are shaken into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Two people waggling the ends of something were doing the twist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Did twist' sounds like the dance; as a past-tense verb it means wrenched an ankle or wrist.
explanation.definitionFit: To sprain a joint is to twist it violently, so sprained matches the past tense did twist.

clue.text: Blokes taking lead from damsel in distress

indicators.note: taking away the lead of a word removes its front letter
something in distress is disordered and upset, so the remaining letters get rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written before its front letter goes

explanation.surface: Chaps step forward to rescue a damsel in distress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Damsel in distress' is a stock phrase, which hides that 'in distress' works on the word alone once its D is gone.
explanation.definitionFit: Blokes is British slang for men, and men are males.

clue.text: Fake suffering's called out - Methuselah's full of it

indicators.note: words that are called out are spoken, so it is their sound that counts

blocks.note: a sham is a fake and pain is suffering

explanation.surface: Someone's pretend agony is exposed, and the setter Methuselah is accused of being full of such falseness.
explanation.walkthrough: Methuselah is the setter's own pseudonym, so the surface reads as self-mockery; but a methuselah is also a giant wine bottle holding eight standard bottles.
explanation.definitionFit: A methuselah is an oversized bottle used chiefly for sparkling wine from Reims and Épernay, so that is what fills it.

clue.text: Illicit recordings of Welsh Greens broadcast

indicators.note: something broadcast is heard over the air, so the sound of the words is what matters

blocks.note: the leek is a national emblem of Wales, a green vegetable

explanation.surface: Secret tapes of the Welsh Green Party are aired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greens' looks like the environmental party; here it means vegetables, and leeks are Wales's emblem.
explanation.definitionFit: Leaks are unauthorised disclosures of confidential material, such as secretly made recordings passed to the press.

clue.text: Museum regularly checked old issues for damage

indicators.note: checking at regular intervals means taking every other letter

blocks.note: the V and A, London's Victoria and Albert Museum
the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: A museum periodically examines its back numbers for signs of deterioration.
explanation.walkthrough: The V and A is the Victoria and Albert Museum in London, often written V&A.
explanation.definitionFit: To vandalise is to wreck property deliberately, so it fits damage used as a verb.

clue.text: Sailor transports hot American fellow to date

indicators.note: to transport is to carry, so the sailor carries the following letters inside him

blocks.note: a tar is a sailor
H for hot, as on a tap
US for American
F is the abbreviation for fellow

explanation.surface: A seaman ferries a heated American man somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: Tar is old slang for a sailor, from the tarred clothing seamen once wore; 'transports' reads as shipping goods but means holding letters inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases mean up to the present moment, as in 'progress so far'.

clue.text: Self-governing Welshwoman's wanting national flowers

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so the letter for the following word is missing

blocks.note: a free state governs itself
Sian is a Welsh woman's name, here possessive
N is the abbreviation for national

explanation.surface: An independent-minded Welsh woman longs for her country's floral emblems.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the N from the possessive name to leave the final four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Freesias are fragrant South African plants of the iris family grown for their blooms.

clue.text: Accomplished director playing character in Romeo and Juliet

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for director
an actor who is playing is on stage
the only letter found in both the name Romeo and the name Juliet

explanation.surface: A skilled director is acting a role in Shakespeare's tragedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' suggests a role in the play, but it means a letter: E is the one letter Romeo and Juliet share.
explanation.definitionFit: Something accomplished has been completed, finished off.

clue.text: Gradually got teeth into Times piece

blocks.note: past tense of bite
by means multiplied by, as in three by four
a bit is a small piece

explanation.surface: Someone slowly gets stuck into a newspaper article in The Times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times' looks like the newspaper but is the multiplication sign read as a word.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means a little at a time, in small stages, which is how something done gradually proceeds.

clue.text: Getting round copyright, provide new arrangement for instrument

indicators.note: getting round something means encircling it, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: to reorder is to arrange afresh
C, from the copyright symbol

explanation.surface: An arranger dodges copyright by writing a new arrangement for an instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting round copyright' sounds like evading the law, but it means placing letters around the copyright symbol's letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The recorder is a woodwind instrument, a simple wooden or plastic flute blown from the end.

clue.text: Opening sections of Howards End lots like Where Angels Fear to Tread

indicators.note: the opening section of each word is its initial letter, so those are kept

blocks.note: the initial letters of the four words

explanation.surface: The start of Forster's Howards End resembles his other novel, Where Angels Fear to Tread.
explanation.walkthrough: Both titles are E. M. Forster novels; his title quotes Pope's 'fools rush in where angels fear to tread', recast here as a place.
explanation.definitionFit: Angels would dread entering the realm of the damned, so the novel title describes the underworld.

clue.text: Krypton possibly brought up halfway through a certain Lois's meal

indicators.note: in a down clue bringing something up raises it, so it reads from the bottom upward
something placed halfway through a word sits in its middle

blocks.note: Lois Lane, Superman's journalist girlfriend; only its outer pieces surround the insert
krypton is an example of a gas

explanation.surface: Superman's home planet Krypton comes up while Lois Lane is half through her dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: Krypton looks like Superman's planet, matching Lois; here it is the noble gas.
explanation.definitionFit: Lasagne is an Italian baked dish of layered pasta sheets, a meal in itself.

clue.text: Downright discontented setter's punching worker's lights out

indicators.note: with its contents gone a word keeps only its outer letters
a punch drives into something, so these letters go inside the worker

blocks.note: its first and last letters
the setter says 'I'm', setter is
a worker is a bee of the class that does the hive's labour

explanation.surface: A thoroughly unhappy setter lands a punch on a labourer and knocks him out.
explanation.walkthrough: The insert goes after the bee's first E: B, E, then D, T, I, M, then the final E. 'Lights out' sounds like a knockout but is a time of night.
explanation.definitionFit: Lights out is the hour, especially in schools or barracks, when everyone must go to sleep.

clue.text: Perhaps the lightest jockey is bet on

indicators.note: to jockey is to manoeuvre and jostle, so the words are pushed into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The lightest rider in a race is the one punters back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jockey' looks like a noun completing 'the lightest jockey', but it is a verb signalling the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone thinnest, with bones showing most, would perhaps weigh the least, hence 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Sirens in the way of ship

blocks.note: à la means in the manner of
Royal Mail Ship, a prefix on ship names

explanation.surface: Mythical sirens lure sailors into a ship's path.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the way of' looks like obstructing the vessel; it means à la, French for in the style of.
explanation.definitionFit: Sirens are warning devices that wail, so they are alarms.

clue.text: Reportedly looks for mistakes in Kafka, Kundera, etc

indicators.note: a report is something told, so the word is judged by how it is spoken

blocks.note: to check is to inspect for errors

explanation.surface: A critic is said to hunt for errors in the works of Kafka and Kundera.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz Kafka was born in Prague and Milan Kundera in Brno, so both writers were natives of Bohemia and Moravia.

clue.text: Service revolver

blocks.note: surface reading: a handgun issued to military or police personnel
setter's reading: a rotating tray that turns round when serving food at table

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is a stock term for a soldier's or officer's pistol; split it as 'service' (serving dishes) and 'revolver' (something that turns).
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a turntable placed in the middle of a dining table so diners can spin dishes toward themselves.

clue.text: What might make you say "don't mention it!" and "less of that!"

definitions.text: What might make you say "don't mention it!" and "less of that!"

blocks.note: the reply prompted by ta, British informal for thank you
the retort prompted by a jeer of disapproval

explanation.surface: A riddle asking what sort of remark draws two familiar retorts, one polite and one sharp.
explanation.walkthrough: Each retort points back to the word that provokes it: thanks for the first, a jeer for the second. Read whole, the clue also defines the answer, a subject that makes people say 'don't mention it'.
explanation.definitionFit: A taboo is a subject socially forbidden, one people are told never to raise in conversation.

clue.text: A bit of heat delineated by weather map

indicators.note: to be delineated by something is to be outlined within it, so the run lies inside the next words

blocks.note: a run spanning the two words

explanation.surface: A small warm patch is drawn on the weather chart.
explanation.definitionFit: A therm is a unit of heat energy, 100,000 British thermal units, used in gas billing.

clue.text: Figure Jung's half-cut when going into Electra complex

indicators.note: cutting half of a word removes half of its letters, here the front half
a complex is a tangled knot, so the letters are jumbled together

blocks.note: the psychiatrist's name, losing its first half
taken as written

explanation.surface: Carl Jung, half drunk, ponders the Electra complex he named.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-cut' is British slang for tipsy, but here it chops JU off. The Electra complex is Jung's term, so the surface hides the anagram signal in plain sight.
explanation.definitionFit: A rectangle is a geometric shape, and a figure in geometry is any such shape.

clue.text: Top journalist ringing gong in lodge

indicators.note: to ring something is to encircle it, so the first piece wraps around the second

blocks.note: the editor is the top journalist on a paper
a gong is British slang for an honour, such as Member of the Order of the British Empire

explanation.surface: A senior editor phones about an honour while staying at a lodge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ringing' suggests a phone call; 'gong' is British slang for a medal or honour, and the MBE is a common one.
explanation.definitionFit: To lodge something is to fix it firmly in place, which is what embed means.

clue.text: Some retired commandos ostensibly not up to much

indicators.note: only some of the letters of the following words are taken, a run within them
to retire is to draw back, so the run is read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: the last two letters of the first word and first two of the second

explanation.surface: Some former commandos apparently aren't much good any more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retired' fits the old soldiers in the surface, which disguises it as the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: So-so means mediocre, middling, which is what 'not up to much' says colloquially.

clue.text: Saint taking on new and unexciting line of work

indicators.note: to take something on is to take it aboard, so the saint holds the next letters inside

blocks.note: St Peter the apostle
N is the abbreviation for new
tame means dull, lacking excitement

explanation.surface: A holy man accepts a fresh but boring job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Line of work' sounds like a career, but it means a line of verse.
explanation.definitionFit: A pentameter is a metrical line of five feet, the kind of line poets build their works from.
